reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: Common hand infections include paronychia (nail fold), felon (pulp space of the fingertip), web space and deep palmar space abscesses, and pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, each with characteristic anatomy
Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci are the usual pathogens, but bite wounds, aquatic exposure, and immunocompromise broaden the range to include anaerobes and atypical organisms

Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis is a surgical emergency recognised by Kanavel's signs: fusiform swelling of the finger, semiflexed resting posture, tenderness along the flexor sheath, and pain on passive extension
Human bite injuries over the knuckle (fight bite) frequently penetrate the joint and extensor mechanism and are notorious for serious deep infection if underestimated
Early localised infections may settle with elevation, splinting, and antibiotics, but established abscesses and closed-space infections require prompt incision and drainage
A felon is a closed-space infection of the fingertip pulp that can raise pressure enough to threaten the tissue and requires timely drainage
Delayed or inadequate treatment of deep hand infection risks tendon necrosis, stiffness, spread along fascial planes, and permanent loss of function
Elevation, splinting in a safe position, and early mobilisation once infection is controlled help preserve hand function
reference.pathophysiology: Hand infections usually follow inoculation of bacteria through a break in the skin from trauma, bites, splinters, or nail-care injury. The hand's compartmentalised anatomy - closed pulp spaces, synovial flexor sheaths, web spaces, and deep palmar spaces - confines infection under pressure and allows it to track along defined planes. Rising pressure within closed spaces impairs perfusion and can cause tissue and tendon necrosis. In pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, pus within the closed synovial sheath compromises the gliding surface and blood supply of the flexor tendon, leading to adhesions and stiffness if not decompressed. Bite wounds introduce mixed oral flora deep into tissues and joints.
additionalDifferentials: Acute gout or pseudogout of the hand
Herpetic whitlow (viral, should not be incised)
Foreign body reaction or retained foreign body
Complex regional pain syndrome or reactive swelling
additionalInvestigations: Inflammatory markers and white cell count to gauge severity
Wound and intraoperative cultures, including for anaerobes and atypical organisms when exposure suggests
Plain radiographs to detect foreign body, gas, retained tooth fragment, or osteomyelitis
Blood cultures if systemic sepsis is present
Ultrasound to identify collections or fluid within the flexor sheath
Joint aspiration and crystal analysis when gout or septic arthritis is considered
redFlags: Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis with Kanavel's signs requiring urgent surgical decompression
Fight bite over a knuckle with possible joint or extensor tendon penetration
Rapidly spreading infection, crepitus, or systemic sepsis suggesting necrotising infection
Deep palmar space abscess or infection tracking proximally along fascial planes
Signs of tissue necrosis or compartment involvement
reference.prognosis: Superficial infections such as early paronychia treated promptly usually resolve fully. Deep and closed-space infections carry a higher risk of stiffness, contracture, and functional loss, and outcome is closely tied to how quickly drainage and appropriate antibiotics are provided. Untreated flexor sheath and deep space infections can lead to tendon necrosis, amputation, or long-term disability.
pitfalls: Underestimating a fight bite and closing or under-treating a wound that has penetrated the joint
Incising a herpetic whitlow, which worsens the viral infection
Delaying surgical drainage of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis while relying on antibiotics alone
Missing a retained foreign body as the source of persistent infection
Failing to elevate and splint, leading to persistent oedema and stiffness
Overlooking gout or crystal arthropathy masquerading as infection
management: Empirical antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci with an anti-staphylococcal penicillin or cephalosporin, broadened with a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor to cover oral anaerobes for human and animal bite wounds
Prompt incision and drainage of established closed-space collections such as felon, paronychia, and web-space or deep palmar space abscesses
Emergency surgical decompression and irrigation of the flexor sheath for pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis to preserve tendon gliding
Elevation, splinting in the position of function, and analgesia, with early localised infection often settling on antibiotics and these measures alone
Formal exploration, irrigation and open management of fight-bite wounds over the knuckle, with tetanus prophylaxis and inspection of the joint and extensor mechanism
Add meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus cover where risk factors exist and atypical or anaerobic cover after aquatic or bite exposure
Hand therapy and serial functional review to limit stiffness and contracture, escalating to theatre if infection spreads or fails to settle
